course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Land-Based Empires
unit.description: Study how gunpowder, administration, and religion helped land-based empires expand and hold power across Eurasia and Africa.

topicQuizzes.title: Comparison in Land-Based Empires topic quiz

firstTopic.title: Empires Expand
firstTopic.summary: How gunpowder weapons, military organization, and rivalries shaped the growth of the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, Qing, and Songhai states.

topic.title: Empires: Administration
topic.summary: How rulers used officials, soldiers, religion, monuments, and taxes to legitimize and consolidate power.

framework.name: InSPECT
framework.title: Use InSPECT to choose your evidence
framework.intro: A fact can connect to more than one lens. Choose the lens that helps answer the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Based on the class Early Religions + InSPECT slides, pages 5-17.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

choices: rejected Islamic law in favor of local customs
used their roles as religious leaders to win European allies

stimulusBlocks.source: busbecq-forster-1881
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, ambassador of the Habsburg ruler Ferdinand I to the court of the Ottoman sultan Suleiman I, letter written in 1555 describing his audience with the sultan, published in Latin in 1589
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Life and Letters of Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, trans. Charles Thornton Forster and F. H. Blackburne Daniell (London: C. Kegan Paul, 1881), vol. 1, Letter I. Project Gutenberg eBook #53629.
stimulusBlocks.note: Spahis were cavalry; Janissaries were infantry recruited through the devshirme. Busbecq's letter was addressed to a friend in the Habsburg lands.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Sultan's hall was crowded with people, among whom were several officers of high rank. Besides these there were all the troopers of the Imperial guard, Spahis, Ghourebas, Ouloufedgis, and a large force of Janissaries; but there was not in all that great assembly a single man who owed his position to aught save his valour and his merit. No distinction is attached to birth among the Turks; the deference to be paid to a man is measured by the position he holds in the public service. . . . Those who receive the highest offices from the Sultan are for the most part the sons of shepherds or herdsmen, and so far from being ashamed of their parentage, they actually glory in it . . . .

This is the reason that they are successful in their undertakings, that they lord it over others, and are daily extending the bounds of their empire. These are not our ideas, with us there is no opening left for merit; birth is the standard for everything; the prestige of birth is the sole key to advancement in the public service.

questions.prompt: The system Busbecq describes is best explained by which Ottoman practice?
choices: The millet system, which let religious communities manage their own affairs
The devshirme, which allowed Muslim nobles to buy offices for their sons
The devshirme, which trained recruits taken as boys to serve the sultan
Tax farming, which sold the right to collect revenue
questions.explanation: The devshirme produced Janissaries and officials who owed their rise to training and the sultan's favor.
choiceExplanations: Religious community self-government does not explain how officials were chosen.
The devshirme recruited Christian boys; it was not a way for nobles to buy offices.
The devshirme produced Janissaries and officials who owed their rise to training and the sultan's favor.
Tax farming concerned revenue, not the selection of officials.
questions.distinguisher: The devshirme is right, but it took Christian boys and excluded the purchase of office by nobles.

choices: his desire to criticize a European system based on birth

choiceExplanations: Peasants paid through local collectors, not to the emperor in person.
Only the Ming reform required silver.
Zamindars and tax farmers kept part of what they collected rather than drawing salaries.
Zamindars, tax farmers, and simplified silver payments were all ways to collect from vast populations.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.2, KC-4.3.I.D: rulers used tribute collection, tax farming, and innovative tax-collection systems to generate revenue
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, comparing tax collection in three empires, c. 1550–1700
stimulusBlocks.text:
Large empires needed steady revenue, and each solved the problem differently. In Mughal India, zamindars, local landholders, collected land taxes from peasants and passed a share to the state. The Ottomans increasingly sold the right to collect certain taxes to tax farmers, who paid the treasury in advance and then collected what they could. In Ming China, reforms in the late 1500s combined many taxes and labor duties into a single payment in silver.

Each method raised money, but each had costs. Intermediaries could keep too much, squeeze peasants, or build local power that rivaled the central government.

questions.prompt: The author's concluding claim in the passage is that
choices: tax systems that used intermediaries always caused the empires that used them to collapse
tax systems that used intermediaries carried risks for rulers and peasants
tax farming was the most efficient system in the world
silver payments ended corruption in Ming China
questions.explanation: The author says intermediaries could keep too much, squeeze peasants, or build rival power.
choiceExplanations: The passage describes risks, not inevitable collapse.
The author says intermediaries could keep too much, squeeze peasants, or build rival power.
The author does not rank systems by efficiency.
The passage does not say silver ended corruption.
questions.distinguisher: The author names risks, but “always caused collapse” is far stronger than the passage claims.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.2, KC-4.3.I.C: rulers used bureaucratic elites and military professionals to consolidate power; salaried samurai are an illustrative example
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how the Tokugawa shoguns governed Japan after 1603
stimulusBlocks.text:
After decades of civil war, Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun in 1603. His successors required the daimyo, the regional lords, to spend every other year in the capital at Edo and to leave their families there when they returned home. This alternate attendance system was expensive and kept the daimyo under watch.

Samurai were moved off the land and into castle towns, where they received fixed stipends paid in rice. Many became administrators rather than active warriors. A strict social order ranked samurai above peasants, artisans, and merchants, even as merchants in cities such as Osaka grew wealthy.

questions.prompt: The Tokugawa treatment of samurai described in the passage was most similar to

the European practice of nobles holding land in return for service
the Mughal use of zamindars to collect land taxes
the Ottoman use of tax farmers to pay soldiers
questions.explanation: Both regimes turned warriors into salaried servants of the central ruler.
choiceExplanations: Both regimes turned warriors into salaried servants of the central ruler.
Samurai lost their land and received stipends instead.
Zamindars were tax collectors, not salaried warriors.
Tax farming was a revenue system, not a way of paying a professional class.
questions.distinguisher: Land in return for service describes how samurai had lived before; Tokugawa policy moved them off the land and paid stipends.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.2, KC-4.3.I.A: rulers used religious ideas, art, and monumental architecture to legitimize their rule
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how rulers used architecture and art, c. 1450–1750
stimulusBlocks.text:
Rulers built on a massive scale to display power. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, using white marble and Persian, Indian, and Islamic designs. The Ottoman architect Sinan designed the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul for Suleiman I. In France, Louis XIV moved his court to the palace of Versailles in 1682, where nobles competed for his attention through elaborate ceremonies.

Such projects were expensive, but they presented the ruler as wealthy, pious, and permanent. They also employed thousands of artisans and turned the capital into a stage for royal authority.

choices: was built as a grand tomb to honor a beloved member of the royal family
served as a working court where nobles competed for royal attention
was built to show the ruler's religious devotion
used designs borrowed from several cultures
questions.explanation: Versailles housed the court and its ceremonies, which kept nobles close to the king.
choiceExplanations: Only the Taj Mahal was a tomb.
Versailles housed the court and its ceremonies, which kept nobles close to the king.
The Taj Mahal is the monument tied to religious devotion here.
The passage stresses mixed designs at the Taj Mahal.
questions.distinguisher: This describes the Taj Mahal, which was a tomb; Versailles was a palace for the living court.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, supporters of divine right argued that
choices: kings should share power with nobles in representative assemblies

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.2, KC-4.3.I.A: rulers used religious ideas to legitimize their rule; European notions of divine right are an illustrative example
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the idea of divine right in Europe, c. 1600–1715
stimulusBlocks.text:
Many European monarchs of the 1600s claimed to rule by divine right, the idea that God chose kings and that subjects owed them obedience as they owed obedience to God. Supporters of Louis XIV, who ruled France from 1643 to 1715, argued that the king answered to God alone, not to nobles or representative assemblies. Louis never called France's old assembly of estates, the Estates-General, and relied instead on royal officials sent to the provinces.

Critics pointed to the costs: long wars and heavy taxes fell hardest on peasants. In England, conflict over royal power led to civil war in the 1640s and the execution of King Charles I in 1649.

questions.prompt: The events in England described in the passage best illustrate
choices: resistance to claims of unlimited royal power
the success of absolutism in every European state
the spread of Islam in western Europe
resistance to royal power led by the Catholic Church
questions.explanation: Conflict over royal power led to civil war and the execution of Charles I in 1649.
choiceExplanations: Conflict over royal power led to civil war and the execution of Charles I in 1649.
England shows that absolutism was contested.
The passage concerns royal power, not Islam.
The English opposition centered on Parliament, not the Catholic Church.
questions.distinguisher: Resistance is right, but the English conflict was led by Parliament and its supporters, not the Catholic Church.

stimulusBlocks.text:
Askia Muhammad seized the Songhai throne in 1493 from the son of Sunni Ali, a ruler whom Muslim scholars had criticized for mixing Islam with local religious practices. Askia Muhammad made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496 and 1497 and returned with the title of caliph's deputy for West Africa. He appointed Muslim judges, supported scholars in Timbuktu, and encouraged Islamic law in the towns.

In the countryside, many farmers and fishers kept older beliefs. Askia Muhammad's Islam strengthened his ties to merchants and scholars, but it did not erase local religion.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.2, KC-4.3.I.C and KC-4.3.I.A: rulers used bureaucratic elites and religious and artistic patronage to consolidate power
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how the Qing dynasty governed China, c. 1650–1750
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Qing kept the Ming bureaucracy and the civil service examinations, so Chinese scholars continued to staff most government offices. At the highest levels, many posts were held jointly by one Manchu and one Han Chinese official. The Kangxi emperor, who ruled from 1661 to 1722, studied the Confucian classics and sponsored large scholarly projects.

At the same time, the Qing required Han Chinese men to wear the Manchu queue hairstyle as a sign of loyalty, and they commissioned portraits that showed emperors as Confucian rulers, Buddhist patrons, and Manchu warriors for different audiences.

The passage says they used several images, not one.
Portraits as Confucian ruler, Buddhist patron, and Manchu warrior each spoke to a different audience.
questions.distinguisher: Confucian imagery was one role among several; the point is that the image changed with the audience.

stimulusBlocks.source: busbecq-forster-1881
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, ambassador of the Habsburg ruler Ferdinand I to the court of the Ottoman sultan Suleiman I, letter written in 1555 describing his audience with the sultan, published in Latin in 1589
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Life and Letters of Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, trans. Charles Thornton Forster and F. H. Blackburne Daniell (London: C. Kegan Paul, 1881), vol. 1, Letter I. Project Gutenberg eBook #53629.
stimulusBlocks.note: Spahis were cavalry; Janissaries were infantry recruited through the devshirme. Busbecq's letter was addressed to a friend in the Habsburg lands.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Sultan's hall was crowded with people, among whom were several officers of high rank. Besides these there were all the troopers of the Imperial guard, Spahis, Ghourebas, Ouloufedgis, and a large force of Janissaries; but there was not in all that great assembly a single man who owed his position to aught save his valour and his merit. No distinction is attached to birth among the Turks; the deference to be paid to a man is measured by the position he holds in the public service. . . . Those who receive the highest offices from the Sultan are for the most part the sons of shepherds or herdsmen, and so far from being ashamed of their parentage, they actually glory in it . . . .

This is the reason that they are successful in their undertakings, that they lord it over others, and are daily extending the bounds of their empire. These are not our ideas, with us there is no opening left for merit; birth is the standard for everything; the prestige of birth is the sole key to advancement in the public service.

questions.prompt: Which Ottoman institution most directly produced many of the officials and soldiers whose rise Busbecq describes?
choices: The timar system, which granted tax revenue to cavalrymen in return for service
The devshirme, which recruited Christian boys to serve as soldiers and officials
The millet system, which let religious communities govern their own affairs
The civil service examinations, which tested candidates on Confucian learning
questions.explanation: Boys taken through the devshirme owed their careers to the sultan, and many rose to be Janissaries or high officials regardless of birth.
choiceExplanations: Timar grants supported cavalry, mostly from established families, not the shepherds' sons Busbecq mentions.
Boys taken through the devshirme owed their careers to the sultan, and many rose to be Janissaries or high officials regardless of birth.
The millet system managed religious communities and did not train officials.
Confucian examinations were a Chinese institution.
questions.distinguisher: Timar holders were an important part of the army, but the officials who rose from humble backgrounds came from the devshirme.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.2 key concept: rulers of land-based empires used art and monumental architecture to display power and legitimacy
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing architecture in land-based empires, c. 1550–1700
stimulusBlocks.text:
Land-based empires used architecture to display their power and faith. The Ottoman architect Sinan designed the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul, completed in 1557 for Suleiman I, with a vast central dome and four minarets. In Persia, Shah Abbas I made Isfahan his capital in 1598 and rebuilt it with a great public square and the Imam Mosque, covered in colored tile.

In India, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in the 1630s and 1640s as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Built of white marble, it combined Persian, Islamic, and Indian decorative traditions. In China, the Qing emperors maintained and expanded the Forbidden City in Beijing as the center of imperial ceremony.

Persian decorative traditions, such as colored tile and refined ornament, shaped both monuments, which celebrated their rulers.
Sinan designed the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul, not these buildings.
questions.distinguisher: Sinan was a famous imperial architect, but his work belonged to the Ottoman Empire.
